title: Understanding Pressures on Threatened Elasmobranchs and Their Drivers to Design Effective Management: Insights From Southern Sumbawa
content:
ABSTRACT

Overfishing of elasmobranchs is a major conservation concern, with large proportions of elasmobranch fishing mortality attributable to incidental catch in small-scale fisheries. Understanding the drivers and impacts of these incidental catches on elasmobranch populations is essential for designing management responses. This study used a mixed methods approach to gather data on incidental catch of threatened elasmobranchs in Southern Sumbawa: An Important Shark and Ray Area (ISRA) in Indonesia. We collated 5 years (2019–2023) of elasmobranch landings data and conducted semi-structured interviews with 31 fishers structured around the Theory of Planned Behaviour. Landings data were analysed to derive simple species- and size-based sustainability indicators and provide insights into fishing pressures by identifying operational and temporal predictors of incidental catch. Interview data were analysed using descriptive statistics to identify underlying socio-economic drivers of catch-relevant behaviour. Our findings were then consolidated around a Driver-Pressure-State-Response (DPSR) framework to propose management responses. Landings data revealed frequent catches of threatened species, with elasmobranch landings dominated by Critically Endangered scalloped hammerheads (Sphyrna lewini) and bottlenose wedgefish (Rhynchobatus australiae), primarily juveniles. The likelihood of catching hammerheads peaks in April, May and December, and is significantly higher for gillnets relative to longlines (p < 0.005). Interview data suggest that fishers do not intentionally target elasmobranchs, but that elasmobranch catches do provide opportunistic additional income. Our findings highlight the need for integrated spatio-temporal and fisheries management within ISRAs to balance urgent conservation priorities with the social and economic importance of small-scale fisheries.
